title: Constrain, validate, and bound model output
summary: Validate structured output, retry with a short repair, cap attempts and tokens, and log without content.

scenario.briefing: The ticket extractor reads support notes and writes JSON for the queue. It once stored priority urgent, retried until the provider rate-limited it, and printed a customer address in the log. Harden the extractor.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.
Review an artifact and identify the concrete risks.

hints: Parse into unknown, then check title, priority, and hours one by one.
Use a for loop with a fixed attempt count instead of while (true).
Pass an output cap to complete and add input plus output tokens to spent.
Log attempt, spent, and title length; never log the note or the reply.

misconceptions.description: Casting parsed JSON to the expected type.
misconceptions.feedback: A cast is erased at runtime. Validate each field and range before the value is stored.

misconceptions.description: Retrying until the model produces valid output.
misconceptions.feedback: A bad model or prompt can fail forever. Cap attempts and tokens, then return a failure.

misconceptions.description: Logging the full prompt or reply while debugging.
misconceptions.feedback: Prompts and replies carry user content. Log identifiers, counts, and lengths instead.

sections.title: A schema is a check, not a type assertion
sections.body: as Ticket compiles but proves nothing at runtime. Parse the JSON, then check each field's type and range before the value reaches the queue.

sections.title: Retries need a stop condition
sections.body: A repair attempt is useful once or twice; an unbounded loop turns a bad prompt into a bill. Cap attempts, cap output tokens per call, and stop when the budget is spent.

sections.title: Evaluation sets make regressions visible
sections.body: Keep a fixed set of notes with expected tickets and run every prompt or model change against it. One passing example is not evidence that extraction works.

sections.title: Logs describe the operation, not the payload
sections.body: Log the event, attempt, spend, and field lengths. Notes and raw replies can contain personal data, so they stay out of logs.

steps.title: Harden the structured extractor
steps.prompt: Edit structured.ts. Validate every field of the model reply, allow at most three attempts with a short repair instruction, stop when the token budget is spent, and log counts and lengths only.

tests.description: Every field of the model reply is checked before it is used.
Attempts are capped and each call has an output limit.
The token budget stops further calls.
A failed validation is reported back without echoing the raw reply.
Logs carry counts and lengths, never the note or the reply.

steps.title: Review the extractor
steps.prompt: Review the extractor and select every real problem.

artifact.title: extractTicket.ts
artifact.caption: The extractor trusts the model reply and retries until it happens to work.

findings.label: JSON.parse is cast to Ticket without checking the title, priority, or hours fields.
The while (true) loop retries with no attempt limit or token budget.
Each call allows 100000 output tokens, so a bad reply can cost far more than the task needs.
The note and the raw model reply are written to the log.
An out-of-range priority is rejected before the value is used.
Malformed JSON is caught and turned into a validation failure.

verdicts.label: Block the change until validation, retries, cost, and logging are fixed.
Ship it; the extractor is safe for production.
Only naming or formatting should change.

steps.explanation: The cast accepts any object, the loop has no attempt or token limit, and each attempt allows a huge reply. The log also writes the customer note and the raw output, which may contain personal data.
